processing: Today a pan-fired flat green made in the manner of Longjing: leaf is spread to wilt for 6 to 12 hours, fixed in a wok, cooled, then pressed flat and dried in a final wok stage.
harvest_season: Around Qingming, with a bud and one leaf or a bud and two just opening; the finest lots are picked about ten days before Qingming.
appearance_dry: Flat, smooth, straight leaves of even size, yellow-green with a soft sheen.
appearance_wet: Tender, even buds and leaves that open into whole little sprays of bright green.
taste_profile: Clean and fresh-scented with a mellow, sweet and brisk finish, and a slight initial bitterness in the older strip-style tea.

brewing.notes: Brew like a Longjing, in a glass or small pot with water well off the boil. Keep the leaf loose in the vessel rather than stewing it.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese greens it is sold as the current spring harvest and is best within a year. Pre-Qingming picking is the premium lot. Genuine temple-area leaf was always a tiny share of the total, so ask where in Daguan the tea was grown.
description:
Cuihua is a small historic green from Daguan county in northeast Yunnan, named after Cuihua Temple on Cuiping Mountain. That makes it an oddity: a flat, Longjing-style tea from a province known for big-leaf teas, grown on a medium-leaf local plant in the cool, cloudy hills at roughly 1100 to 1400 metres.

The tea changed shape in the twentieth century. The old temple tea was sun-dried and curled into rings, which earned it the name Jin'erhuan, 'golden earrings'. What you buy now is usually flat and straight, pressed by hand against a warm wok after a long wilting, the method copied from Hangzhou.

In the cup it is yellow-green and clear, with a fresh fragrance and a mellow sweetness rather than the sharper edge many Yunnan greens have. Treat it gently: cooler water and a roomy vessel keep it sweet, and hot water brings out a bitterness it does not need.

It is rarely seen outside Yunnan. Look for the spring date and the county on the pack, and remember that 'Cuihua' may also cover the curved strip style called mei cha, which is a different cup from the flat one.
history:
Local accounts differ on how old it is: some claim more than 500 years, while the fuller histories tie it to monks at Cuihua Temple planting a few dozen good bushes in the Yongzheng reign of the Qing. Those accounts also say it went as tribute, including to the Empress Dowager Cixi, and that monks carried it on pilgrimage to Emei, and that it won a second-class honour at the 1915 Panama exposition; these claims come from county-level histories and are hard to check.

The modern tea dates from the 1950s. Nie Aizhong, a tea graduate from Hangzhou assigned to Daguan in 1955, helped found the Cuihua tea factory that year, adding a proper kill-green step and replacing sun-drying with baking, and an imitation Longjing was added after a 1957 move. The flat tea went by the name Longjing until 1980, when it was renamed Cuihua Tea, and it was then listed among Yunnan's provincial famous teas in the early 1980s.
